questions.q: Write the structures of the two main products formed when phenol is treated with dilute nitric acid at 298 K, and explain why they can be separated by steam distillation.
questions.a: The products are o-nitrophenol (intramolecular H-bonding, steam volatile) and p-nitrophenol (intermolecular H-bonding, less volatile). A wrong answer that draws m-nitrophenol reveals the student does not understand the ortho/para directing effect of –OH. Writing both products but giving incorrect reasoning for steam distillation (e.g., "o-nitrophenol has higher boiling point") shows confusion between intra- vs intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol without any Lewis acid catalyst, whereas benzene requires FeBr₃ for bromination.
questions.a: The –OH group donates electron density into the ring via resonance, making the ring highly electron-rich and activating it toward electrophilic attack. The phenoxide ion formed in water is even more activated. A wrong answer stating "–OH is electron-withdrawing" or "bromine water is a stronger electrophile" reveals fundamental misunderstanding of activating groups and the role of catalysts in electrophilic aromatic substitution.

questions.q: Predict the major product when 3-methylphenol (m-cresol) undergoes mononitration. Draw the structure and justify the position of substitution using resonance structures.
questions.a: Major product: 2-methyl-4-nitrophenol (nitro group para to –OH, ortho to –CH₃). The –OH is strongly activating and ortho/para directing; –CH₃ is weakly activating and ortho/para directing. Positions ortho to both groups (C-2 and C-6) are most activated, but C-6 is sterically hindered by –CH₃, so substitution occurs at C-4 (para to –OH). A wrong answer placing nitro at C-6 (ignoring sterics) or C-5 (meta to –OH) shows inability to weigh directing effects and steric factors.

questions.q: Compare the reactivity of phenol, phenoxide ion, and anisole (methoxybenzene) toward electrophilic aromatic substitution. Rank them in increasing order of reactivity and explain using resonance structures.
questions.a: Order: anisole < phenol < phenoxide ion. Anisole: –OCH₃ donates by resonance but inductive withdrawal reduces net donation. Phenol: –OH donates by resonance, no inductive withdrawal from alkyl group. Phenoxide: negative charge on oxygen enhances resonance donation dramatically. A wrong ranking (e.g., phenol < anisole) reveals confusion between inductive and resonance effects of alkoxy vs hydroxy groups.

questions.q: A student writes the following equation for Kolbe's reaction: C₆H₅OH + CO₂ + NaOH → o-HOC₆H₄COONa. Identify two errors in this equation and write the correct balanced equation with proper reaction conditions.
questions.a: Errors: (1) Phenol must first be converted to sodium phenoxide with NaOH before reacting with CO₂; the equation shows direct reaction of phenol. (2) The reaction requires heating under pressure (400 K, 4-7 atm), not room conditions. Correct: C₆H₅ONa + CO₂ → (400 K, 4-7 atm) → o-HOC₆H₄COONa. A student missing the phenoxide step shows they don't understand the reaction proceeds via the more nucleophilic phenoxide ion.

questions.q: Design a two-step sequence to convert phenol to 2,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde using reactions covered in this chapter. Specify reagents and conditions for each step.
questions.a: Step 1: Kolbe's reaction — phenol + NaOH → sodium phenoxide, then CO₂ (400 K, 4-7 atm) → salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) after acidification. Step 2: Reimer–Tiemann reaction on salicylic acid — CHCl₃ + NaOH → 2,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde (formylation ortho to –OH, para to –COOH). A poor answer attempting direct Reimer–Tiemann on phenol gives only salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde), missing the second –OH introduction. This reveals inability to plan multi-step synthesis using directing effects.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Phenols undergo ______ aromatic substitution reactions where the –OH group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles to ortho and para positions via resonance donation of the oxygen lone pair into the aromatic π-system, making phenols far more reactive than benzene toward nitration, halogenation, sulfonation, and Friedel–Crafts reactions.

Fill in the blank: Observe how a few drops of bromine water added to phenol in a test tube instantly form a white precipitate of 2,4,6-______ — a reaction so fast it needs no catalyst, unlike benzene which requires FeBr₃.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can predict the major product(s) of nitration, halogenation, sulfonation, and Friedel–Crafts reactions of phenol and substituted phenols, explain the ortho/para directing effect using resonance structures, and distinguish reaction conditions that give mono- vs poly-substituted products.
